podcast.body: From The Wailers' 1973 album "Burning," this song never charted in the US Top 40 for Marley himself, but it became the only song he wrote to reach number one when covered by Eric Clapton in 1974. Marley later explained it was a song about justice, crafted to avoid issues with directly writing about shooting police, although his former girlfriend Esther Anderson controversially suggested it was about birth control. "The only song that Marley ever wrote that did make it to number one is I shot the sheriff. Of course Eric Clapton is the one who covered that and took it to number one."

podcast.body: Written around 1972 and released as a single in February 1973, this song appears on the surface to be about a person on the run from the law after shooting a sheriff. Bob Marley himself stated it was a metaphor for justice, and he initially wanted to say "I shot the police" but changed it to "sheriff" to avoid issues with the Jamaican government. However, his former girlfriend, Esther Anderson, maintains it's a protest against contraception, arguing that Marley viewed birth control pills—which she was seeking at the time—as an abomination to his Rastafari beliefs, and that "Sheriff Brown" is a veiled reference to a doctor who "kills a seed before it grows." "Bob sings Sheriff Brown always hated me for what I don't know. Every time I plant a seed, he said, kill it before it grow."
